33e1d7779a:70d7c8fb68ff246d.title: AI campaign deepfakes are starting to draw legal threats
33e1d7779a:70d7c8fb68ff246d.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:70d7c8fb68ff246d.summary: Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-Wis.) was hit with a cease-and-desist letter this week over an AI deepfake he posted falsely depicting his Democratic opponent voicing positions her campaign says she rejects. Why it matters: Van Orden is the latest in a growing number of candidates and elected officials facing legal complaints and threats over AI deepfakes in campaign ads. Driving the news: Attorneys for Rebecca Cooke, Van Orden's Democratic opponent, sent him a cease-and-desist letter on Wednesday over his "pattern of posting misleading AI-generated videos that falsely attribute statements to Cooke." The letter singled out an August X post by Van Orden showing an AI-generated Cooke saying she wants to "take advantage of as much corruption as possible and give every illegal alien free healthcare" — something she never said. Van Orden's team didn't respond to Axios' request for comment, but he responded to Cooke publicly with an AI-generated video of a duck wearing a Democratic Socialists of America T-shirt, yelling, "cease and desist." The big picture: AI deepfakes have proliferated this election cycle, while Congress has yet to establish a federal standard governing their use. Some campaigns have used hyperrealistic ads. Texas Senate GOP nominee Ken Paxton combined real and inaccurate statements from his opponent, James Talarico . In Louisiana's Republican Senate primary, one candidate was shown busing undocumented immigrants to polling places. Others have used more cartoonish ads that candidates have said are intended as parody. About 31 states regulate political deepfakes, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, including at least 28 that require disclosures for AI-generated content. Zoom in: Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick (R) faced a criminal complaint from his Democratic opponent, state Rep. Vikki Goodwin, in September under Texas' deepfake election law. The law says AI-ads cannot be aired within 30 days of an election if the intent is to influence…

33e1d7779a:ccba07dc1e57859f.title: Trump expected to tap DNI Jay Clayton as new AI czar
33e1d7779a:ccba07dc1e57859f.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:ccba07dc1e57859f.summary: President Trump is expected to tap Jay Clayton , his director of national intelligence, for a new role as the White House's artificial intelligence — or in Trump's words, " super intelligence " — czar. Why it matters: Clayton, who Trump previously told Axios would be a good idea for AI czar, is expected to take on the second title, sources told Axios. Calls for government intervention into AI's rapid development are growing, but the president has repeatedly said he favors a light regulatory touch and has called fears about the tech's threat to humanity a hoax . Trump had been warming to the idea of tapping Clayton, who as DNI has shown that he sees the security threats AI poses as serious. Driving the news: Trump could make the announcement as soon as Friday, sources familiar confirmed to Axios. A White House official said in a statement to Axios that "[a]ny personnel announcement will be announced directly by the President. Any reporting until then is baseless speculation." Catch up quick: Asked by Axios earlier this week who he wants to be AI czar, Trump said: "I have somebody in mind." Clayton is "a good man. He's right here. That's a good idea," Trump added when prompted. Zoom out: Trump announced last month that he'd create an "AI Force" and would soon name a new AI czar, but offered few details on what the Force would do. Since then, he's huddled with several titans of the AI industry — some of whom have been key voices in advocating for a slowdown of the tech . Flashback: Clayton was elevated to be Trump's principle intelligence adviser atop the 18-agency intelligence community earlier this year after his prior DNI, Tulsi Gabbard, resigned in May. Previously the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Clayton's qualifications received bipartisan blessings. After sidestepping questions over who won the 2020 election during his confirmation, Clayton was confirmed on party lines, without Democratic support. Go deeper: Trump's call for "AI Force"…

33e1d7779a:7dc9ef8aa7d3d2e7.title: Pope Leo says AI lacks the "spark of humanity" — and wants artists and the church to fight back
33e1d7779a:7dc9ef8aa7d3d2e7.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:7dc9ef8aa7d3d2e7.summary: Pope Leo XIV called Friday for the church to form an alliance with artists to protect human creativity during an era of AI-generated content. Why it matters: Though he has acknowledged the technology's potential benefits, the pope continues to warn that AI progress cannot come at the expense of human dignity. The statement comes after the New York Times reported on Anthropic's efforts to confer with religious scholars to infuse religious morals into Claude. What he's saying: "In this era of artificial intelligence, it is becoming urgent to distinguish human art from what machines produce," the pope wrote on X. "There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others. Algorithms lack the spark of humanity." Leo said the Catholic Church is calling for "an alliance with artists and cultural institutions to safeguard our humanity." Zoom out: Leo has spoken out against AI before, specifically around how the technology could influence and potentially harm humanity. In the first encyclical of his papacy, he said there was a need to "disarm" the technology to prevent it "from dominating humanity." In May, the pope established a Vatican commission on AI to coordinate the church's policies and work around the technology. Last week, he warned of a "paradise of machines" invading and taking over our daily activities. He also said that recent warnings from AI researchers should be "taken seriously." "We have to keep working. We can't sit back and pretend nothing is going to happen," he told reporters in late September. Flashback: The late Pope Francis also warned that AI potentially risked reducing humans into data points.

33e1d7779a:dfe8ea3ded2ccdbe.title: What to watch in the Supreme Court's big climate case
33e1d7779a:dfe8ea3ded2ccdbe.author: Ben Geman
33e1d7779a:dfe8ea3ded2ccdbe.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday will hear arguments in a case that could determine the fate of state-court lawsuits nationwide seeking climate damages from oil giants. Why it matters: Billions and billions of dollars are at stake for the oil industry in dozens of cases brought by state and local governments. Governments face mounting costs from climate change that litigants link directly to the companies' products. The big picture: SCOTUS is considering whether federal law blocks damage claims under state laws for the effects of interstate and global emissions. State of play: It's specifically about litigation against Exxon and Suncor that the city and county of Boulder filed in 2018. But dozens of state-court cases are active in California, Connecticut, New York, Massachusetts and beyond. The cases aren't identical. But overall they accuse oil giants of concealing risks or making deceptive statements, and seek damages for climate-related costs. Here are a few big themes and dynamics ahead of Monday morning: This is a blockbuster. The decision will be the culmination of an intense, years-long battle (unless it's not, but more on that in a moment). There's a high level of organizing, lobbying and advocacy among industry and climate advocates alike around these state cases. Industry and allied groups say the wave of cases threatens oil companies' very ability to operate. It's a sign that both sides see litigation as a critical battleground on climate. Take a spin through the case docket and you'll see what I mean. A kicked can is possible. SCOTUS might not decide the question of federal preemption. That's because it's also considering whether it even has jurisdiction right now. The question turns on whether a Colorado Supreme Court decision to let Boulder's case proceed in state court can be reviewed at this stage. Trump policies are a new(ish) wrinkle. U.S. and industry briefs argue that addressing an interstate and global topic with these state claims is preempted by…

33e1d7779a:27b019c05e966bda.title: Behind the Curtain: AI's existential legal crisis
33e1d7779a:27b019c05e966bda.author: Mike Allen
33e1d7779a:27b019c05e966bda.summary: No industry has ever documented its own foreseeable risks as loudly as AI. Imagine a plaintiff's lawyer reading the public warnings of Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: They told the world it was dangerous. They told the world it was moving too fast. Then they unleashed it and sold it to your kid. No industry has ever taken so much copyrighted work and left behind so much proof. Imagine a plaintiff's lawyer reading OpenAI's own files to a jury: They trained on a pirated library. They renamed it to something blander. Then they deleted it when the headlines got hot. Why it matters: AI's origins, use and future will be picked apart in countless epic court fights, with a historic paper and public statement trail to tap. Every significant invention — be it social media, automobiles, electricity or capitalism itself — gets disrupted and eventually shaped by the courts. AI, with its tentacles into every part of industry and life, will experience this at scale. The big picture: The fights are no longer theoretical. They're underway, in discovery and headed toward juries. Early verdicts and settlements capture the risk for the biggest players. 🤖 Chatbots are being treated as products, not speech. Unlike social media companies, they likely can't hide behind Section 230 , which protects platforms from liability for what users post — not what the platform itself creates. 📖 Copyright is a massive problem. Anthropic already paid the biggest copyright settlement in history, $1.5 billion to authors and book publishers, and now music publishers and news media want a piece. 💻 Agents gone wild. What happens when they do damage — and it was foreseeable and foreseen? ⚖️ Discovery gone wild. AI leaves LOTS of receipts (and, ironically, makes it easier for the lawyers to comb through them, too). Product liability turns on two words: foreseeable and knew. Punitive damages turn on whether you knew the danger and shipped anyway. This is where all these memos and warnings could really backfire.…

33e1d7779a:e583d6e66d738db0.title: Inside the AI industry's grassroots rebellion, led by elite researchers at frontier companies
33e1d7779a:e583d6e66d738db0.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:e583d6e66d738db0.summary: A small cadre of elite AI researchers is wielding extraordinary influence inside OpenAI and other leading companies, challenging executives, shaping policy and complicating negotiations with Washington. Why it matters: As a safety crisis has unfolded across the industry, it's an open question who is doing more to shape the national AI debate — top researchers or the executives they report to. The researchers, some of whom are among the most highly paid and sought-after scientists in the world, are outspoken online and have repeatedly clashed with company strategy. The big picture: The situation has the makings of a grassroots uprising, where any potential deal the companies may strike — with the Trump administration, one another, or even globally — will also have to pass muster with their top scientists. Behind the scenes : OpenAI, Anthropic and others at the frontier of AI aren't like other companies. Many began years ago as idealistic research labs with scientific cultures that prized openness and collaboration. To function, and to continue to build better and better models, the companies need highly specialized machine learning researchers and scientists to push the frontiers of what's technologically possible. The trouble is , the best of those researchers are in extraordinarily short supply. Last year's talent wars drove compensation packages into the hundreds of millions of dollars for the most elite, giving top researchers enormous leverage over their employers. Perks include favorable vesting schedules for their compensation and largely freewheeling policies that allow them to share triumphs, trash rivals and offer their perspectives about the AI race frequently on X. AI CEOs must prioritize safety and embrace regulation to retain top research talent, an OpenAI investor told Axios. Zoom in: OpenAI President Greg Brockman scrapped plans to donate another $25 million to a pro-AI political group that some researchers had openly criticized. Researchers and…

33e1d7779a:aa66af201f39d918.title: Why Washington and Tehran keep talking past each other
33e1d7779a:aa66af201f39d918.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:aa66af201f39d918.summary: The Trump administration and the Iranian regime both say they prefer a diplomatic solution to the war , but a deal looks more elusive than ever. The root causes of the impasse may be irreconcilable. Why it matters: In the last 18 months, two failed rounds of negotiations have led to two wars. The June MOU collapsed within days and led to renewed escalation. If the current effort to reach a diplomatic breakthrough ends in a deadlock, another outbreak of fighting is likely within weeks. Here's a look at some of the deep-seated dynamics between the two countries — personal, cultural, and political — that have stymied efforts to broker a deal: "Trump has ADD; Iran has OCD" One reason for the failures is that the U.S. and Iran see the timeframe for negotiations very differently. Trump is all about getting a quick deal — he gets impatient and frustrated when things move slowly. The Iranian negotiation style is the complete opposite. They are all about playing for time. "America under Trump is the attention-deficit superpower ... incapable of sustaining a strategy. Iran under the Islamic Republic is the obsessive-compulsive theocracy, fixated on resisting America far more than advancing the welfare of its own people," Karim Sadjadpour, a senior analyst at the Carnegie Endowment, told Axios. "Trump has ADD; Iran has OCD." For example, in April 2025 Trump set a deadline for negotiations at 60 days — an extremely short and unrealistic timetable. The Iranians, on the other hand, saw the negotiations as a longer process and didn't take the deadline seriously enough. They didn't think Trump meant it when he said 60 days. The negotiations in February of this year were even shorter — around three weeks. The chances of getting a deal that quickly were close to zero. A megadeal vs. a narrow truce Trump loves a splashy show of political theater, with him cast as lead actor. He envisions a legacy-making accord that redefines the relationship between the U.S. and Iran and reshapes…

33e1d7779a:f651498cb25a706c.title: "Strange bedfellows": Bernie Sanders, Florida Dems and a benchmark $250k donation
33e1d7779a:f651498cb25a706c.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:f651498cb25a706c.summary: MIAMI — Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders is sending the Florida Democratic Party $250,000. It's a relative pittance in the Sunshine State — but the check signals a big political shift. Why it matters: The state party's moderate leaders have resisted the rising tide of democratic socialists elevated by Sanders for years. But political changes and financial need have brought the two together like never before: The Florida Democratic Party is essentially broke after decades of being out of power, and national establishment Democratic organizations have so far refused to help. Angie Nixon , who joined the Democratic Socialists of America this summer, is the state party's U.S. Senate nominee. Sanders endorsed her and has long wanted to help, an aide said. Zoom in: Despite being vastly outraised and outspent in Florida, Nixon and Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly are stubbornly close in polling to their respective Republican opponents, Sen. Ashley Moody and Rep. Byron Donalds. Until now, national Democrats have been hesitant to spend in Florida due to years of soul-crushing defeats —especially at the hands of President Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis — that made the state and its 10 expensive media markets look like a bad investment. This year, with Republican fortunes sagging nationwide, Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska look more promising for Democrats. That could change soon. Nixon told a liberal podcaster Thursday that the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, held a fundraiser for her. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), whom Nixon called out last week for not helping, also might make money available. "Folks are a little gun-shy because, unfortunately, Vice President [Kamala] Harris lost as a Black woman. And so people are being very hesitant in terms of funding Black women, especially in the South," Nixon told MS NOW's "Clock It with Symone & Eugene." Behind the scenes: Florida Democratic Party chair…

33e1d7779a:30df9d634cf990bc.title: "We're not asking for charity": Wikimedia CEO calls out AI for unpaid data use
33e1d7779a:30df9d634cf990bc.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:30df9d634cf990bc.summary: Wikipedia is starting to feel the effects of the AI-driven shift in how people find information, with page views falling 8% in the latest year, new Wikimedia Foundation CEO Bernadette Meehan tells Axios. Why it matters: Wikipedia is a crucial source of information for AI models, but those same models increasingly allow people to get Wikipedia-derived information without ever visiting the site — potentially threatening the ecosystem that keeps the online encyclopedia running. Driving the news: Wikipedia page views declined 8% in 2025, and while the drop wasn't unexpected, "that doesn't mean that we're sort of starry-eyed about it and not concerned about it," Meehan said. Follow the money: The problem is that even though generative AI systems rely heavily on Wikipedia's vast trove of human-created information, some companies won't pay for it, she said. Wikimedia has a program that charges large-scale commercial users for reliable, high-volume access to its data. Publicly disclosed enterprise customers, whose payments make up 10% of the organization's operating expenses, include Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Perplexity and others. OpenAI and Anthropic, two of the largest makers of generative AI models, aren't among Wikimedia's publicly disclosed enterprise customers. Meehan noted that Wikimedia has other agreements that aren't publicly disclosed and declined to identify those companies. OpenAI and Anthropic both declined to comment. What they're saying: Meehan, a former U.S. ambassador to Chile who took over Wikimedia's top job in January, said the reception from big technology companies has been mixed. Some have embraced the idea that companies benefiting from Wikipedia should help sustain it. Others, she said, have acknowledged what Wikimedia considers excessive use of its data but declined to pay for enterprise access. "We're not asking for charity," Meehan said. Between the lines: There's an unusual economic tension here: Wikipedia makes its content freely…

33e1d7779a:9a303b8b4d65bd13.title: Scoop: U.S. sent more Patriots to protect Saudi, Qatari energy sites
33e1d7779a:9a303b8b4d65bd13.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:9a303b8b4d65bd13.summary: The U.S. military in recent weeks sent two additional Patriot missile batteries to protect oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, two U.S. officials and one regional source said. Why it matters: The U.S. wanted to reassure both allies that it would protect their key energy facilities in case President Trump decides to resume major combat operations against Iran. Trump said on Thursday that he's considering renewing a bombing campaign in the coming weeks. "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said. Flashback: In early August, when Trump was considering launching a massive attack that included strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure, the leaders of both Saudi Arabia and Qatar lobbied him not to do it. They expressed grave concern that Iran would strike their oil and natural gas facilities in retaliation. U.S. officials said the pleas were a key reason Trump decided not to attack and move instead toward an economic pressure campaign. Behind the scenes: Last month, the U.S. military sent one additional Patriot battery to Saudi Arabia to protect a key oil facility. Another Patriot battery was sent to Qatar to protect a natural gas facility. The U.S. will need Saudi Arabia to allow it to use the country's airspace if major combat operations resume. But the Saudis are unlikely to grant permission if they feel oil facilities won't be protected. A spokesman for U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), Capt. Tim Hawkins, declined to comment. Reality check: Patriot batteries and especially their interceptors have become a highly sought-after commodity since the war in Iran started. The U.S. military transferred batteries and interceptors to the Middle East from other regional commands, raising concerns about readiness in other parts of the world. State of play: The U.S. military is sending more warships, fighter jets and troops to the Middle East ahead of a possible resumption of the war. A U.S. official said the USS…

33e1d7779a:1ecdde15091aa400.title: House Democrats' behind-the-scenes pitch for dues: Help us take on MAGA Inc.
33e1d7779a:1ecdde15091aa400.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:1ecdde15091aa400.summary: House Democratic leadership is pointing to the colossal spending by President Trump's super PACs in their behind-the-scenes efforts to get members to pay their dues to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee , Axios has learned. Why it matters: DCCC dues have fueled heated infighting among House Democrats in recent months, with several proposals emerging to force members to cough up more money. Some House Democrats want to require colleagues to pay their dues before seeking committee leadership roles, as The Washington Sun first reported . But other lawmakers, particularly in the Progressive and Black Caucuses, are "furious" about these suggestions, said a senior House Democrat, who told Axios that "members ... don't like threats." Driving the news: "While our case to the American people is strong, our Frontliners and candidates face ugly daily attacks from the right as MAGA Inc. unloads its coffers," DCCC chair Suzan DelBene (D-Wash.) wrote in an email to House Democrats obtained by Axios . "We need the resources to fight back and support our battleground colleagues and candidates in these final weeks," she added. DelBene ended the email with a plea for dues payments: "I urge everyone to make a dues contribution today. Let's make sure we don't have any regrets on Election Day." Between the lines: While several House Democrats noted to Axios that DelBene routinely urges members to pay their dues — in emails and at caucus meetings — some clocked a more urgent tone than usual. One lawmaker described the email, which was sent out on Wednesday, as "slightly more aggressive about shaming people" about not paying their dues than past entreaties. By the numbers: A pair of super PACs linked to MAGA Inc. have emerged as two of the top spenders on congressional races nationwide despite launching in September. No Going Back PAC and Safety and Affordability PAC have respectively spent $50 million and $38 million on ads in House races, according to ad tracking firm…

33e1d7779a:db8217b009123b05.title: Scoop: Dems beef with party leaders over snubbed Black candidates
33e1d7779a:db8217b009123b05.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:db8217b009123b05.summary: Democratic House leaders are being pressured by their members over the lack of Black candidates receiving top-level party support in the final weeks of the 2026 midterms, Axios has learned. Why it matters: With 33 days to go, Democrats are torn between triaging their resources and satisfying all corners of their party's diverse but fractious racial coalition. Zoom in: Some Black lawmakers have taken their concerns to Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and DCCC chair and Rep. Suzan DelBene (D-Wash.) about the lack of Black candidates on the DCCC's " Red to Blue " list, according to a senior aide to a House Democrat. Congressional Black Caucus Chair Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.) spoke personally with DelBene about the lack of Black candidates on Red to Blue, according to two sources familiar with the matter. The intrigue: The dearth of Black representation was a hot topic of conversation among legislators at the Congressional Black Caucus' annual conference in D.C. in September, three people told Axios. "Members were openly talking about it, and they were pissed," said one Democratic operative. "Red to Blue" provides fundraising and staffing assistance to contenders in swing districts. The intrigue: Their push comes as some legislators argue that Democrats should do more to support Black candidates in the wake of a recent Supreme Court ruling that could threaten Black representation in Congress. Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), a CBC member, told Axios that "with the CBC under attack through gerrymandering and voter suppression, it's essential that the party invest in Black candidates." In particular, she urged the DCCC to help Justin Pearson, a Black candidate running in a long-shot bid for Tennessee's 9th House District. "Justin Pearson is an exceptional candidate who has proven that coalition-building and community-centered campaigns can make strides — even with the odds stacked against him," she said. "He is exactly the type of candidate the DCCC should be…

33e1d7779a:1b5bc5f56561f122.title: Mortgage rates approach 3-year high as new applications plunge
33e1d7779a:1b5bc5f56561f122.author: Nathan Bomey
33e1d7779a:1b5bc5f56561f122.summary: Mortgage rates spiked to their highest level in nearly three years, continuing their climb above the 7% threshold. Why it matters: Housing sales were already slow due to a lack of inventory and elevated rates, creating a risk that the market could further its freeze. Zoom in: The weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.28% as of Thursday, Freddie Mac reported . That's up 0.94 points from a year ago, and up 0.25 points from last week. Mortgage rates closely track 10-year Treasury yields, which have risen by over 1.25 percentage points since the start of the Iran war in February. The impact: Mortgage applications are plunging. The Mortgage Bankers Association reported Wednesday that applications during the week ended Sept. 25 fell 6% from a week earlier. With rates at their highest point since November 2023, home buyers are beginning to turn to adjustable-rate mortgages. ARMs made up 10.3% of mortgage applications in the most recent period, marking the highest point since October 2025, according to MBA. "Affordability and borrower demand have weakened in recent weeks as the higher-rate environment continues to put pressure on both prospective homebuyers and homeowners looking to refinance," MBA CEO Bob Broeksmit said in a statement. What we're watching: There are early signs that rising rates could put downward pressure on prices as sellers look to attract buyers. "Softer market conditions and greater affordability pressures have contributed to increased pricing pressures across many of our markets," KB Home senior VP William Hollinger said last week on an earnings call, noting the home builder had "made pricing adjustments." Reality check: Rates may not remain elevated for long. "We expect the situation to improve next year, as energy prices drop back and the aggressive Fed tightening cycle which has been priced into money markets does not fully materialise, causing mortgage rates to retrace most of their recent increases," Capital Economics senior North…

33e1d7779a:85ad898550c03414.title: Lawyers: Pike getting "life-saving care" after failed execution
33e1d7779a:85ad898550c03414.author: Adam Tamburin
33e1d7779a:85ad898550c03414.summary: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike's attorneys said she was "in critical condition" and "receiving life-saving care" Thursday, a day after she survived an execution attempt during which the state administered two doses of the lethal injection drug. A death penalty expert told the Associated Press that Pike's survival after receiving the execution drug was unprecedented. The latest: State and federal elected officials are pressing for public accountability after the second failed execution this year. Gov. Bill Lee ordered a independent review of the Pike execution attempt. On Thursday morning, he told reporters there were "very few answers" about what had gone wrong. U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the frontrunner to succeed Lee as governor next year, blasted the "botched process" in a statement and pushed for the state to "bring back the electric chair." Pike's attorneys told reporters Thursday that Lee's pledge to launch an investigation did not go far enough. They urged him to commute her death sentence. What they're saying: Attorney Randy Spivey, who was inside the prison during the execution attempt, said prison officials spent about an hour trying to establish IV access. He counted at least seven needles used in Pike's left arm alone. Pike complained of sharp pain during the lethal injection. Spivey said he noticed her right arm turning purple, especially after the second round of chemicals. He said the lawyers had also been told of blistering and burning around the injection sites. Between the lines: Federal public defender Stephen Ferrell said the lawyers had warned courts months earlier about medical problems with Pike's veins that made it harder to establish an IV. Zoom in: The attorneys also said they weren't able to quickly reach their colleagues or court officials responsible for overseeing the execution. Spivey said it took seven minutes and passage through six locked doors to get to a telephone so he could reach the rest of Pike's legal team.…

33e1d7779a:405bd7244fb12908.title: Christa Pike's execution failed. Here's how lethal injection works
33e1d7779a:405bd7244fb12908.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:405bd7244fb12908.summary: Lethal injections are under scrutiny after Christa Pike survived two rounds of drugs during Tennessee's failed attempt to execute her. Why it matters: Lethal injection has been the dominant U.S. execution method for decades, accounting for roughly 89% of the 1,683 executions carried out since 1976, per the Death Penalty Information Center . Driving the news: Pike , convicted of killing a classmate three decades ago, survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs Wednesday in what would have been the state's first execution of a woman in 200 years. In response, Gov. Bill Lee halted executions and ordered a "comprehensive, third-party review" of the failed attempt. Pike's execution attempt followed hours of legal whiplash in which courts first stayed the execution before reversing course. Pike is still alive as of Thursday afternoon, her attorney said at a news conference, according to the AP . She is receiving "lifesaving care" after a failed attempt Wednesday night that her attorney said amounted to "torture." The big picture: Execution protocols vary by state, but lethal injections generally follow the same basic process. Here's what to know. Why states adopted lethal injection Flashback: Lethal injections emerged after the Supreme Court allowed capital punishment to return in the 1970s. Oklahoma became the first state to authorize the practice in 1977. Texas carried out its first five years later. Before lethal injections, states commonly used methods like electrocution, gas, hanging and firing squads. Lawmakers considered injections to be less violent and cheaper. Lethal injections are now used in all death penalty states. The Supreme Court requires states to reserve the death penalty only for the most heinous murders. Several states — Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah — allow firing squads . Idaho made firing squad its primary execution method in July. How lethal injections are administered There isn't one standard procedure. States use…

33e1d7779a:ce76d8f811642c1c.title: Netanyahu: Omani co-pilot went through Islamic radicalization
33e1d7779a:ce76d8f811642c1c.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:ce76d8f811642c1c.summary: The initial investigation into the attempted hijacking of the FlyDubai flight from the UAE to Israel found that the co-pilot went through religious Islamic radicalization in recent months, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News Thursday. Why it matters: Netanyahu's remarks, confirmed by an Israeli intelligence official and people who worked with the co-pilot, strengthen the possibility that the incident was a terrorist attack. Driving the news: The investigation is being led by the Saudi security services, which have been interrogating the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the other pilot while the plane was en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The United Arab Emirates has formed a team to investigate the incident. "The investigation includes examining all circumstances and motives surrounding the incident, including any possible connection to terrorist activity or intent, and whether it involved prior planning or direction," a spokeswoman for Emirati Foreign Minister Afra Alhameli said in a statement . Behind the scenes: An Israeli intelligence official said the Mossad and Shin Bet spy agencies are also investigating. "The Omani co-pilot went through a process of religious radicalization in recent years. We don't know yet if he is a 'lone wolf' or whether he was sent by someone to conduct an attack," the official said. The intrigue: On Wednesday, Israel's Channel 16 reported testimony of another FlyDubai pilot who knew the Omani co-pilot. According to the report, the co-pilot worked for the company for only eight months and was more religiously observant than most of his co-workers. What he's saying: President Trump told reporters Thursday he has reason to believe Iran was involved in the foiled hijacking. "Based on what I'm hearing is yes, but we're working on it right now," he said. Israeli officials say they currently don't have indications of Iranian involvement, by they haven't ruled it out. The Saudi Ministry of Interior said in a statement that…

33e1d7779a:3b60d491466fa823.title: British Iranian arrested in U.K. terror plot probe
33e1d7779a:3b60d491466fa823.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:3b60d491466fa823.summary: A U.K. Iranian dual national was arrested on suspicion of preparing to carry out terrorist acts in connection with an incident at an English air base used by the U.S., British counterterrorism police said Thursday. The big picture: Tehran has denied any involvement in the suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford, while U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in it. Driving the news: The 27-year-old man was arrested in Westminster, London, on Thursday afternoon on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006, per a Counter Terrorism Policing statement . Police also questioned a 26-year-old British man and searched two properties in the area. Five men in their 20s, who were arrested on Sunday following the early morning incident remain on police bail, according to the statement. Context: The British government earlier this year allowed the U.S. to use RAF Fairford for limited defensive strikes against Iranian missile capabilities. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps noted in July that U.S. B-1 bombers flew from RAF Fairford and said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory is a legitimate target for us." State of play: Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans in a statement described the investigation into circumstances surrounding the incident in Gloucestershire as "hugely complex." Specialist teams are "interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," she said. "As we've made clear, we're looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement." Context: The British government earlier this year allowed the U.S. to use RAF Fairford for limited defensive airstrikes against Iranian missile capabilities. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps noted in July that U.S. B-1 bombers flew from RAF Fairford as it said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory is a legitimate target for us." What we're…

33e1d7779a:cb1bf3ba82e5539d.title: The Fed's long-term interest rate problem
33e1d7779a:cb1bf3ba82e5539d.author: Neil Irwin
33e1d7779a:cb1bf3ba82e5539d.summary: The relentless rise in long-term interest rates is starting to have effects on more parts of the economy, Kansas City Fed president Jeff Schmid told Axios Thursday. "You're starting to see some friction in some of the long-market users of credit," he said, pointing to multifamily housing and commercial lending. "Even on the mortgage rate side, it's starting to affect home prices, which is how the price of credit works relative to valuation," Schmid said at a conference on investing in rural America hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond in Asheville, N.C. The big picture: Schmid spoke alongside Richmond Fed president Tom Barkin and Boston Fed president Susan Collins, who weighed in on the forces driving the rise in borrowing costs. "I think you're seeing this trillion-dollar AI buildout, and I think it's not surprising that rates go up if you've got a lot more demand out there," Barkin added. Collins said AI investment is also helping drive the solid economic growth that has persisted despite higher borrowing costs. "I think it does have broader effects, not just in particular sectors," Collins said. But it "remains to be seen" whether investment will continue at its current pace, she added. The intrigue: Schmid likened the Fed's challenge of separating strong demand from supply-driven inflation to a seven-layer dip — one of his favorite foods. "The beauty of a seven-layer dip is you have equal amounts of beans and sour cream," Schmid said. Right now, with AI and data centers, "there's too much beans in that dip," he added. "And not enough chips!" quipped Barkin.

33e1d7779a:5d0debc277d190a9.title: The world opinion shifts on tariffs
33e1d7779a:5d0debc277d190a9.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:5d0debc277d190a9.summary: More countries are buying into a core piece of President Trump's argument about what is broken in global trade, even as his tariffs rattle the world economy. Why it matters: Two major agreements over the past month show that more countries are embracing the view that huge trade imbalances and excess production can hurt domestic industries and may warrant action. Driving the news: G20 trade officials are in Milwaukee this week, where they announced a new agreement to tackle the global steel glut. The "Milwaukee Framework" calls on countries to curb market-distorting subsidies and step up monitoring of steel imports and trade circumvention. It also endorses "evidence-based actions" against excess capacity, including possibly tariffs. That agreement follows a broader acknowledgment at the G20 finance ministers meeting in Asheville, N.C., in September. The U.S. and nearly every other G20 economy there agreed that large, persistent trade imbalances can harm other countries. They signed on to a statement that asked nations with big surpluses to address policies that leave them overly reliant on exports for growth. China was the lone G20 member present to object to that statement. Between the lines: For decades, governments have warned about distortions in global trade, including excess steel production. What is changing: the willingness to acknowledge the damage to domestic industries and protect them. "Most countries agree with these global issues, people agree with the diagnosis, but they're loath to action," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters on the sidelines of the conference. He said the Milwaukee agreement "couldn't have happened in 2015." "All these other countries — they know that if they want to continue to have access to the U.S. market, we need to adjust the international system," Greer said. "As we come with creative ideas and new structures and cohesive plans, they're coming on board." Zoom out: EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič welcomed…
