33e1d7779a:79249a9eed9796fe.title: 5 takeaways from Trump's combative Time interview
33e1d7779a:79249a9eed9796fe.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:79249a9eed9796fe.summary: President Trump's 75-minute interview with Time revealed his latest thinking on the Iran war , the AI race (or in his words, SI), the media and more. Why it matters: The interview with one of America's most historic news publications gives voters insight into the direction of the country roughly a month ahead of the midterms. Driving the news: Trump was unapologetic across the board: on prolonging the Iran war, resisting AI regulation and threatening to "go after" Democrats if they win the House. The interview was historic, too, as it was Trump's 56th appearance on a Time cover, "surpassing President Richard Nixon, who held the record for more than half a century," the magazine says . Here are five takeaways. Trump on Iran: Trump was defiant when asked why the war in Iran had stretched longer than the timeline he originally floated, telling Time, "I could have stopped then, but I wanted to go further." He said the press "fed" Americans his initial prediction of attacks lasting around four to six weeks, a timeline he gave to multiple outlets at the start of the war. He also repeatedly suggested the war was almost over . He reiterated the threat he made before the UN General Assembly that he may "annihilate" Iran. Pressed to square that with the assertion that he's the president of peace, Trump replied, "by annihilating Iran, we've created peace in the world." He also said it's "possible" he'd ramp up bombing after the midterms, disputing Pentagon reports of a munitions shortfall. Trump on Netanyahu reelection: Trump sidestepped questions about whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should be reelected in Israel, with the election just weeks away. He said he was "not involved in politics anymore" but touted his popularity in Israel. Pressed again, Trump applauded U.S. support for Israel, saying, "No, my primary thing—I do want to help them defend Israel." On Netanyahu's leading opposition candidate and former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot,…

33e1d7779a:fb5c1b2e0f0abb25.title: The rocky road to a new permitting law
33e1d7779a:fb5c1b2e0f0abb25.author: Ben Geman
33e1d7779a:fb5c1b2e0f0abb25.summary: A sweeping bipartisan deal to cut permitting red tape faces a long road ahead despite a broad show of support. Why it matters: Cutting hurdles for energy projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors, but some green groups fear erosion of safeguards. Powerful business groups want to make building all sorts of infrastructure easier. Driving the news: Top Republicans and Democrats on the Senate's energy and environment panels on Wednesday dropped the 417-page bill that includes: New limits on the duration of lawsuits, and the scope and length of reviews under the Clean Water Act and National Environmental Policy Act. A stronger federal hand in siting and approval of large transmission projects. Protections for previously issued permits, a priority for renewables groups and Dems upset with Trump administration barriers. The big picture: A who's who of major business and energy industry groups — representing oil and gas , renewables and coal — cheered the bill. The White House backs the deal and wants quick passage, an official said. State of play: The deal still has a long road ahead. Co-author Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) said Wednesday at a press conference that there will be revisions as backers seek input from colleagues. There are also "unresolved" questions about Trump officials returning to "regular order" for wind and solar projects, Whitehouse said. But he credited the administration with a "very reasonable opening proposal" on the matter. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), the top Democrat on the Natural Resources Committee, criticized the bill and said his party will have a stronger hand next year. Center-left backers see a huge opening to help build out clean energy and grid upgrades to integrate it. But groups on the left flank of the climate movement panned it , calling it a giveaway to fossil fuel interests. What we're watching: Some groups with close ties to Democrats staked out a noncommittal-to-positive position, saying they…

33e1d7779a:da5f950018447add.title: Trump, Big AI go all-in together
33e1d7779a:da5f950018447add.author: Zachary Basu
33e1d7779a:da5f950018447add.summary: President Trump and the AI industry have co-signed one of the biggest economic and technological wagers of all time. If it goes right: A new age of abundance — explosive productivity, staggering wealth and a generational leap in American power. If it goes wrong: A catastrophic bust that destroys capital, jobs and, in the words of several involved, threatens widespread human harm . Why it matters: Neither Trump nor the AI titans have plausible deniability. Their fortunes have become so tightly bound that success will be shared — and failure impossible to disown. The big picture: Trump and Big AI have fused their futures around four enormous bets. 1. The economic bet: That trillions poured into chips, data centers and power will create a productivity engine powerful enough to fuel a new Industrial Revolution. AI infrastructure spending is projected to reach $10.3 trillion by 2032, but the payoff remains unproven : one analysis found hyperscalers have spent nearly $1 trillion more on AI since 2024 than AI has generated in revenue. The promise sold by Trump and his tech allies is a new era of growth and abundance. The peril is a historic misallocation of capital on a scale few industries have ever seen. 2. The regulation bet: That Washington can clear the runway for an AI takeoff while leaving the companies largely responsible for policing themselves. The new White House accord signed by Trump and the AI giants enshrines voluntary safeguards, company-led testing and third-party reviews instead of new federal mandates. The promise is American dominance over China. The peril is that self-regulation fails, forcing Washington to intervene only after damage has already been inflicted. 3. The safety bet: That AI can grow vastly more powerful without becoming vastly harder to control. Many of the most dire safety warnings come from AI researchers themselves. Anthropic's own IPO prospectus contemplates scenarios in which advanced AI kills humanity. The promise is almost…

33e1d7779a:3bc96ec27c59c8cb.title: Trump and CEOs try to shed AI's toxic branding
33e1d7779a:3bc96ec27c59c8cb.author: Dave Lawler
33e1d7779a:3bc96ec27c59c8cb.summary: The great AI rebranding is on, led by President Trump and tech titans like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who are embracing an alternative term: "Superintelligence," or SI. Why it matters: Leaders in D.C. and Silicon Valley are worried the public backlash against AI and data centers will hamper the development of this staggeringly powerful and existentially dangerous technology. The new label is part of a broader effort to shift the narrative. Driving the news: Flanked by the most powerful figures in tech on Tuesday, Trump officially declared "superintelligence" the preferred terminology of the executive branch. He'd previously solicited alternative terms for AI on Truth Social. "Now we're calling it, again, super. We can say the word super, because the other word is a fake word," Trump said after Tuesday's White House summit. Leaders from Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI and Nvidia all signed the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence." Huang has recently extended the label to physical infrastructure, referring to data centers as "superintelligence factories." Opposition to the huge, energy-guzzling facilities is dimming the prospects for fast-growing AI firms and some congressional candidates. Between the lines: A rose by any other name would smell as sweet, and AI by any other name will likely seem as scary. Communities are building bipartisan coalitions against data centers, younger workers are anxious about their career prospects, and AI insiders continue to warn about catastrophic risks, notes Axios Communicators author Simon Hernandez-Arthur. Calling it "super intelligence" attempts to evoke the technology's promise without immediately bringing to mind all that negative baggage. What they're saying: Some of the tech executives who appeared with Trump continued to use "AI" in their remarks, but xAI CEO Elon Musk caught himself and pivoted to "SI." Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has long used the "superintelligenc" branding. Huang, CEO of the world's most valuable…

33e1d7779a:0a5e1073e5cb277a.title: How Trump's signature issue fell off voters' radar
33e1d7779a:0a5e1073e5cb277a.author: Brittany Gibson
33e1d7779a:0a5e1073e5cb277a.summary: Immigration — the issue that helped propel Donald Trump to the presidency and rally his supporters over the past decade — has become an afterthought for voters. Why it matters: It's another ominous sign for Trump and the GOP heading toward November. What was once a rallying cry for the party is losing salience with voters across the spectrum — and harsh crackdowns have even made it a liability among some Republicans. "On net, Republicans win out as the more trusted party on only two topics, and it's border/immigration [and] crime and safety," said Avery James of Echelon Insights, a Republican polling firm. "But the problem if you're a campaign strategist is quite simple: crime and immigration are just not the top issues for voters." The big picture: Just two years ago, immigration was a top concern for voters nationwide, especially self-identified Republicans. After President Biden dropped his reelection bid, the GOP spent half its advertising budget on immigration-related ads, per an AdImpact analysis . "If you ask [about] immigration as an overall issue that people care about, it went from like a top three issue two years ago to way down the list now, in single digits," said Erik Iverson, a GOP pollster working with the Republican Senate campaign arm. Between the lines: Pollsters say concern about immigration peaked during Biden's tenure, when illegal border crossings and asylum seekers at the Southern border surged. But weeks into Trump's term, crossings dropped dramatically after he deployed the U.S. military at the border, instituted a ban on asylum claims and paused refugee admissions. "You become a victim of your own success," Iverson said. Zoom in: Cost of living ranks as the top issue for voters, far outpacing immigration. That's especially bad news for Republicans trying to turn out voters in competitive statewide races. More than half of Texas Republicans and one-quarter of independents said border security and immigration was Texas's most important…

33e1d7779a:a40df220edfd67b7.title: GOP senators endure painful week with little to show for it
33e1d7779a:a40df220edfd67b7.author: Stef W. Kight
33e1d7779a:a40df220edfd67b7.summary: Exhausted GOP senators are preparing to fly home mostly empty-handed after staying in D.C. longer than expected. Why it matters: The midterm outlook is getting bleaker by the day, and Republicans have a monster to-do list for the lame-duck session that could be a last chance to capitalize on their trifecta. Between the lines: Republicans decided against breaking for an early recess last week. The biggest thing to show for it: A historic — and bipartisan — college sports package that doesn't do much for those defending their seats in November. It faces long odds in the House. 😖 Otherwise it was a week of pain: Failed votes: A vote addressing Americans' concerns about data centers driving up energy costs failed today, as did another to curb congressional stock trades and enforce voter IDs. A line of attack that backfired: A major hearing with Jack Smith was overshadowed by a failed attempt by Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) to link the special counsel and Atlanta prosecutor Fani Willis. The Trump issue: Republicans have been tiptoeing around whether Trump's unpopularity will hurt the party in November, only for Texas nominee Ken Paxton to be caught blaming Trump's midterm convention for hurting his polling. NRSC Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said Paxton's analysis was "just wrong" and called the convention "a boost in the right direction." 🤕 Zoom out: Some of the GOP senators are returning to fresh campaign headaches. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) lost a week of in-state campaigning and didn't even get a vote on one of her key priorities: a bipartisan bill to lower insulin costs. Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) is the target of a new ad campaign hitting him over his pardon of a man who pleaded guilty to first-degree sexual assault. Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) has been batting down accusations that he went after mothers of new babies over unpaid medical bills. His lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter to his opponent — Rev. Adam Hamilton — on Monday. The GOP has a cash advantage ,…

33e1d7779a:d65100d555cca810.title: Scoop: Rubio ordered Iranian delegation to leave the country, U.S. official says
33e1d7779a:d65100d555cca810.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:d65100d555cca810.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio demanded on Monday that the Iranian delegation to the United Nations General Assembly immediately leave the country after negotiations stalled, according to a U.S. official and a second source with knowledge of the matter. Why it matters: Though the Iranians were likely to depart soon anyway, Rubio's move was a highly unusual diplomatic rebuke and laid bare the deep distrust between the two countries amid fruitless efforts to broker an end to the war. Qatari mediators tried to secure a diplomatic breakthrough between the U.S. and Iran but made little progress, with neither side willing to budge. Among those ordered to leave New York was Rubio's Iranian counterpart, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. What they're saying: "Secretary Rubio kicked out the Iranian delegation who had overstayed their welcome. The UN General Assembly was over, so it was time for them to go," the U.S. official said. Behind the scenes: On Monday morning, the White House thought there might be progress in talks with Iran later in the day. But by late afternoon it became clear negotiations were at a stalemate. Then on Monday evening, at Rubio's orders, the U.S. mission to the UN told the Iranian mission to the UN that Araghchi's delegation had to leave New York immediately, according to the U.S. official. The Iranian delegation, including Araghchi, left for the airport several hours later and boarded a flight from New York to Doha at 1:20 a.m. Tuesday. A second source confirmed that the U.S. demanded that the Iranian delegation leave, but said Araghchi was scheduled to travel back to Tehran on Monday night anyway. What's next: Qatari mediators are continuing to talk to both sides about their compromise proposal, regional sources say. "Maybe I will blow 'em up," President Trump told reporters on Wednesday when asked how he can reach a deal with a regime he says is crazy. "Maybe I blow 'em up. We have to make that decision. We will blow 'em up or make a deal. But…

33e1d7779a:e9f29209bd6c2a00.title: Netanyahu says FlyDubai pilots prevented a "9/11 disaster"
33e1d7779a:e9f29209bd6c2a00.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:e9f29209bd6c2a00.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu revealed new details about a FlyDubai flight bound for Israel during which a pilot stabbed a colleague, sending the plane spiraling thousands of feet. The big picture: Netanyahu told CNN Wednesday evening that the Indian pilot who was stabbed, Capt. Smit Machchhar, unlocked the cockpit after being attacked and an Israeli passenger who works as a plumber, Yaniv Hayun , entered and found the Omani pilot apparently trying to interfere with the aircraft's controls. Netanyahu said the suspect was being interrogated in Saudi Arabia and that the UAE agreed Israel could participate in the interrogation. What they're saying: The Israeli prime minister told CNN's Jim Sciutto that passengers heard shouts and screams coming from the cockpit and that the plumber saw the attacking pilot hovering over the instruments, noting "he was trying to jam the instruments." The plumber pulled back on the aircraft's controls, while another passenger and crew member subdued the attacker, according to Netanyahu. Reserve pilots then came in and stabilized the plane. Netanyahu said he met Hayun at the airport and that the passenger was "drenched" in the Indian pilot's blood. President Trump said Netanyahu and others had briefed him on what happened. He called the stabbed pilot a "hero" for managing to open the cockpit door and also praised the plumber's actions. Flashback: Netanyahu noted his own history with hijackings: He was wounded while taking part in the 1972 Israeli commando raid that freed passengers from a hijacked Sabena flight. His brother Yoni was killed four years later while leading the Entebbe hostage rescue. Reality check: Netanyahu made clear that investigators don't have any specific information that Tehran had anything to do with this incident. The bottom line: "Those pilots managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster, because that's what it looks like was happening," Netanyahu said.

33e1d7779a:8fbc7513213eb292.title: AI safety fears put OpenAI and Anthropic in the FTC's crosshairs
33e1d7779a:8fbc7513213eb292.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:8fbc7513213eb292.summary: The Federal Trade Commission is investigating OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI companies over potential safety risks posed by their products, an agency spokesperson told Axios Wednesday. Why it matters: The federal government has largely taken a hands-off approach to regulating AI , but the FTC investigation could signal a shift for the industry. Driving the news: FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson is preparing civil investigative demands that would compel AI executives to turn over documents and testify about the safety of their models, according to the New York Post, which first reported the news. The probe has been underway for weeks, predating OpenAI's disclosure that models it was testing escaped their sandbox and compromised parts of AI platform Hugging Face's production infrastructure. OpenAI announced Monday that it would halt the release of its newest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, after it performed poorly on safety testing. ChatGPT maker OpenAI and Claude maker Anthropic did not respond to Axios' request for comment. Between the lines: The recent push by top AI executives for increased guardrails around their technology has prompted some AI critics to question their motives. Ferguson recently said that AI firms are trying to panic Americans into pressuring policymakers to build a regulatory "moat" that would allow AI frontrunners to block smaller competitors from catching up. Catch up quick: News of the ongoing investigation comes just a day after top AI companies sent representatives to the White House to sign a pledge with President Trump to self-police their AI development. Trump compared it to something of a "constitution," but the rules the companies agreed to are similar to what they were already doing. Zoom out: The new reporting comes shortly after Axios exclusively reported that OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers were investigating tens of thousands of potential security incidents, including some that had not previously been disclosed to the public. That…

33e1d7779a:7d0b2815c6cab541.title: Ask Trump's AI chatbot who won in 2020. You might not get an answer.
33e1d7779a:7d0b2815c6cab541.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:7d0b2815c6cab541.summary: The Trump administration's new AI service gave users conflicting responses to politically sensitive questions Tuesday and Wednesday: sometimes answering them and sometimes refusing. The big picture: As the Trump administration increasingly uses AI and answers the public's questions through America.gov, statements carrying the government's authority are shaped by models, instructions and guardrails the public can't see. The White House told Axios in a statement, "America.gov will continue to be updated to provide Americans the most accurate and reliable federal information and resources." America.gov , powered by Google's Gemini and Elon Musk's Grok, aims to help Americans navigate government-related tasks using an AI chatbot — but it quickly drew attention for another reason: It was debunking some of President Trump's long-standing claims. Driving the news: On Tuesday, Axios — like other outlets — found America.gov contradicted the president on the 2020 election and the Jan. 6 attack. It also confirmed former President Obama was born in Hawaii, contradicting the "birther" conspiracy theory Trump spent years promoting . Screenshots: Andrew Pantazi, Avery Lotz/Axios Yes, but: By Wednesday morning, some users were getting a different response: The chatbot refused to answer, saying it did not provide "political commentary." That's what I was told when I asked who won in 2020, around 9:15am: "I only answer questions about U.S. government services and official information. I do not provide political commentary, including election results." I received similar answers about Jan. 6 and Obama's birthplace. Screenshot: Avery Lotz/Axios One editor, using Chrome in New Jersey, asked the same questions on his desktop and also received refusals to answer. However, other colleagues got different results. For example, from Northwest Arkansas, on Chrome: Biden won the 2020 election. Screenshot: Herb Scribner/Axios What they're saying: There are several plausible explanations for…

33e1d7779a:bc77035e22473458.title: Musk returns to Trump world for Pentagon war study
33e1d7779a:bc77035e22473458.author: Colin Demarest
33e1d7779a:bc77035e22473458.summary: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Anduril Industries founder Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich will lead a Pentagon study of the future of warfare dubbed "Project Meridian," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday. Why it matters: It's Musk's first official role advising the Trump administration since his very public feud last year with President Trump after departing DOGE. He has since reconciled with Trump. Driving the news: Hegseth unveiled Meridian during his second address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia. "We are leveraging a unique source of American advantage, one our adversaries do not have: our innovators, our senior leaders and our technologists — big thinkers and doers who will forecast the creative solution for tomorrow's conflicts," Hegseth said . Meridian, he added, is not meant to produce new policy documents. Instead, it will examine "the domains we must conquer, and capabilities we must master." "Their work will be focused on discovering, developing and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes." Zoom in: Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael will help facilitate the project. Michael, speaking to reporters in December about America's industrial base, said he would like to see "five more Andurils and Palantirs and SpaceXs" flourish. What they're saying: "Americans have always been at our best when we bring our smartest scientists, engineers and technologists together to solve the hardest problems in national security," Luckey told Axios. "Together, we will not only study the wars being fought today but also think seriously about the wars we cannot afford to fight in 2030, 2050, and 2100 — and what America needs to build now to prevent them." Follow the money: Musk's and Luckey's respective companies have big Pentagon contracts. SpaceX serves as America's national-security launch backbone, while Anduril furnishes jammers, interceptors, rocket motors and…

33e1d7779a:0e71478fb8311514.title: Fed watchdog clears former chair Powell in renovation probe
33e1d7779a:0e71478fb8311514.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:0e71478fb8311514.summary: A Federal Reserve watchdog found no criminal wrongdoing by former chair Jerome Powell in its investigation of the central bank's expensive headquarters renovation, according to a report released on Wednesday. Why it matters: The findings effectively clear Powell after the Justice Department opened an unprecedented criminal investigation into then-Fed chair, which became public in January. What they're saying: "At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the U.S. Attorney General," the Office of Inspector General wrote in the report. The watchdog added that it "did not identify administrative misconduct during our evaluation." Yes, but: While the report clears Powell, it faults Fed management and oversight of the project as construction costs more than doubled to $2.5 billion . The Fed "did not take numerous actions available to it that could have better controlled costs and mitigated some of the significant construction cost increases," the report says. Flashback : The renovation became a flashpoint in President Trump's broader campaign against Powell and the Fed. Trump toured the construction site with Powell in July 2025 and publicly challenged him over the project's soaring costs. Zoom out: The Justice Department's investigation centered on Powell's June 2025 testimony to Congress about the renovation and its rising costs. Powell denied wrongdoing and argued at the time that the investigation was part of a broader effort to pressure the Fed over interest rates. DOJ closed the investigation in April as the Fed's inspector general continued its review. Zoom in: The watchdog said that inflation alone could not explain the project's higher costs. For instance, the report shows that two major mechanical, electrical and plumbing contracts more than tripled to $539 million from an earlier $178 million estimate, far outpacing the broader rise in construction…

33e1d7779a:94a832095aec3f95.title: Google unveils long-awaited Gemini 4
33e1d7779a:94a832095aec3f95.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:94a832095aec3f95.summary: Google is unveiling its long-awaited next-generation AI model, Gemini 4 Argon, to a small group of cybersecurity partners, the company said Wednesday. Why it matters: Gemini 4 arrives after a long gap at the top of Google's model lineup, in which the company kept rolling out smaller, cheaper Flash models while rivals OpenAI and Anthropic sprinted forward. State of play: Google says Gemini 4 Argon is built to handle complex, long-running tasks in software engineering, finance, legal work and cybersecurity. Google said the new model is state of the art on certain coding and knowledge work benchmarks, outperforming competing OpenAI frontier model GPT-6 Astra on several. The company is rolling the model out only to a group of trusted cybersecurity defenders and is participating in the U.S. government's voluntary pre-release process. Google says it will expand access after additional testing, with paying subscribers first in line. What they're saying: "Argon is a well-rounded model that has frontier capabilities across several domains," Tulsee Doshi, head of Gemini products at Google DeepMind, told Axios. "We've seen strong performance up close as Googlers have put the model through its paces in recent weeks, with many relying on it for their hardest coding and research problems." Flashback: Gemini 4 comes out nearly a year after the previous flagship model generation, Gemini 3. In May, Google CEO Sundar Pichai said the company's next major model release would come in June. That model, widely expected to be Gemini 3.5 Pro, never came out. In July, Axios reported that poor morale among Google DeepMind employees was part of the reason for the delay. Zoom in: Google's additional time investment may not be viewed as negatively in the context of the AI safety debate that has embroiled companies and users. OpenAI has had issues with agents going rogue, and recently said it is scrapping GPT-6.1 Astra due to security issues . Top AI developers OpenAI and Anthropic are…

33e1d7779a:07ae79d44b17cdeb.title: Trump's DOJ takes its fight with federal judges to Minnesota
33e1d7779a:07ae79d44b17cdeb.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:07ae79d44b17cdeb.summary: The Justice Department filed a complaint against a group of federal judges from Minnesota for speaking to The New York Times about the impact of the immigration enforcement surge on their court. The big picture: The complaint opens a new front in the Trump administration's standoff with federal judges, bolstered by a loyal Justice Department. Driving the news: The complaint , which was brought against two jurists who spoke on the record with the paper and those who spoke anonymously, alleged the behavior was "improper and unethical" and called for the judges to be recused from any DHS-related matters. It further urged the Eighth Circuit to investigate. The chambers of the named senior district judges, Patrick J. Schiltz and John R. Tunheim, did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:b8dc65d341da268f.title: Hegseth accuses media of treason in pugnacious annual address
33e1d7779a:b8dc65d341da268f.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:b8dc65d341da268f.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth took aim at the U.S. media during a speech at a Marine Corps base in Virginia on Wednesday, saying: "Our so-called press makes Iranian state media look reasonable." Why it matters: Hegseth cast news outlets as a threat to U.S. troops, escalating his attacks on journalists over reporting based on classified information . What he's saying: In his second annual "State of the Force" address at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, Hegseth accused some members of the media of "treason." While a free press is important, he said "partisan activism that intentionally smears the troops and the historic mission that they're undertaking is fundamentally anti-American. It's sick. It's a national betrayal. It's treason, actually." "It's your movements and bases that they reveal to the enemy," he said. "Ultimately, it's your lives they put directly at risk when they lie about munition stockpiles." Between the lines: Media reports about dwindling supplies of key munitions amid the war with Iran have drawn the ire of President Trump and his team. Hegseth frequently attacks the press and has taken unprecedented steps to restrict the media's access to the Pentagon. Driving the news: Hegseth returned to many culture-war themes in the speech, highlighting his efforts to reverse DEI and gender equity efforts in the interest of "meritocracy." "We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that — no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors." Zoom out: Hegseth also made substantive news in the speech. He confirmed plans for a 20% reduction in generals and admirals across the force, while rejecting descriptions of the cuts as a purge. "As usual, what the media levels as an accusation, I wear as an accomplishment," he said. Hegseth also announced a new Autonomous Warfare Command, an initiative to study the future of war that will involve Elon Musk, and a nationwide competition to…

33e1d7779a:42edc528977d1348.title: Exclusive: HHS launches project to speed up clinical trials
33e1d7779a:42edc528977d1348.author: Caitlin Owens
33e1d7779a:42edc528977d1348.summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday is launching an effort to reimagine the way clinical trials are designed, with a goal of drastically reducing the time and money it takes to develop new drugs. Why it matters: The program, shared first with Axios, could provide a template for reconfiguring the drug development process and boosting U.S. competitiveness in the global biotech race. Driving the news: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health Director Alicia Jackson are unveiling the new effort in Austin, Texas. CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz and FDA Acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas will also attend the announcement. The effort — dubbed the Simulation-augmented, Real-time Platform Adaptive Seamless Trials (SURPASS) program — features teams selected through a bidding process that will bring drug candidates through experimental clinical trial processes. How it works: The initiative under ARPA-H will begin by soliciting ideas from "teams" that include a drug sponsor. Winners will receive funding and support over five years. ARPA-H is looking for proposals that innovate in three technical areas: Phaseless trials that allow faster trials with fewer patients, the ability to analyze data in real time during the trial instead of than only when it ends, and using automation to reduce inefficiencies. Teams will also likely include medical centers or other clinical sites, biostatisticians, and companies that have the ability to predict drug outcomes via a computer. The FDA has been included in the planning of the program, and "there won't be any surprises for regulators in this," said Daria Fedyukina, the program manager. The big picture: One of the reasons China has become such a popular location for drug manufacturers is because it's much cheaper and faster to do early-stage clinical trials there. Experts and the biopharmaceutical community largely agree that in order to compete, the U.S. needs to streamline its trial processes.…

33e1d7779a:ca6a33812f10e419.title: Jack Smith faces new lawsuit over congressional phone records
33e1d7779a:ca6a33812f10e419.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:ca6a33812f10e419.summary: Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sued former special counsel Jack Smith Wednesday, alleging he unlawfully obtained her cellphone toll records during his investigation of Trump and the 2020 election Why it matters: The lawsuit escalates Republicans' efforts to challenge Smith's investigation more than a year after his probe ended. What they're saying: "Through his Arctic Frost witch hunt that targeted conservatives across America and even the President of the United States, Jack Smith perpetrated one of the worst abuses of government power in our nation's history," Blackburn said. "This lawsuit is solely about holding Mr. Smith accountable and ensuring that our nation's justice system can never again be weaponized against the American people. I thank the New Civil Liberties Alliance for their partnership in filing this complaint and for fighting to uphold our cherished constitutional rights." Driving the news: The suit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee one day after Smith testified at a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing Tuesday. The suit alleges Smith obtained a nondisclosure order without telling the judge that the underlying subpoena sought the records of a sitting senator. Blackburn's cellphone provider was ordered to keep the subpoena secret. Blackburn is asking the court to award her $1 in nominal damages to emphasize that she isn't seeking money but instead wants to hold Smith accountable for his allegedly unlawful actions. Legal counsel for Smith did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Flashback: The lawsuit comes one day after Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.), a potential running mate for JD Vance in 2028, accused Smith of perjury at Tuesday's hearing but got his facts wrong and was later corrected by Smith and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.). The mistake went viral and drew extensive criticism on social media. Catch up quick: In October 2025, the GOP-led House Judiciary Committee released highly redacted…

33e1d7779a:61b47fb7fcf6b130.title: 944 children abused by Catholic clergy, Mass. AG says — but no new charges
33e1d7779a:61b47fb7fcf6b130.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:61b47fb7fcf6b130.summary: The Massachusetts attorney general released a report Wednesday documenting more than 270 Catholic clerics accused of sexually abusing 944 children across three dioceses — but the investigation will result in no new indictments. Why it matters: The dioceses created an illusion of safety while church leaders repeatedly exploited loopholes to protect the institution's reputation, systematically concealing staggering levels of abuse. What they're saying: "We deeply understand that behind every number is a child whose safety was violated, a family that was changed, and a survivor who has carried the trauma of that abuse for years, and in many cases, decades," Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell (D) wrote in the report . Catch up quick: The Massachusetts AG's office began its investigation in 2019, examining church responses to abuse allegations over more than six decades. Boston Globe reporters exposed widespread abuse and institutional cover-ups in the Archdiocese of Boston in the early 2000s. Wednesday's report sought to provide the first comparable public accounting of what happened in the Roman Catholic dioceses of Fall River, Springfield and Worcester. Investigators reviewed more than 300,000 pages of documents and interviewed more than 100 people, including survivors, attorneys and clergy. Worth noting: After reporters uncovered the abuse, Massachusetts lawmakers criminalized the reckless endangerment of children and expanded mandated reporter requirements to include clergy. But those laws can't be applied retroactively to crimes that occurred before they took effect. Most of the abuse detailed in the report occurred before 2002, and the AG says newly found misconduct fell outside applicable statutes of limitations. Many accused clergy are also dead, leaving survivors with few options for legal recourse. Zoom in: The report concluded that diocesan leaders actively covered up abuse allegations before 2002 by transferring accused clergy to new congregations…

33e1d7779a:a76f9753c5841668.title: "Strong indications" Iran had role in U.K. bomb plot, PM Andy Burnham says
33e1d7779a:a76f9753c5841668.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:a76f9753c5841668.summary: U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there are "strong indications that Iran played a part" in a suspected bomb plot at a British air base used by the U.S. The big picture: Burnham's comments to the BBC come after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the weekend incident at RAF Fairford "clearly involves the hands ‌of a foreign actor." Tehran denies any involvement. Five British men were released on bail Monday following their arrest a day earlier in connection with the alleged plot. What they're saying: "We will say more in due course but we can confirm ... that we believe Iran to have played a part," Burnham told the BBC, declining to elaborate. He emphasized that the counter-terrorism investigation is ongoing and "complex" and that investigators are "working closely with our colleagues" in the U.S. Rubio told Fox News Monday that the incident "ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world — and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally." Context: U.K. earlier this year allowed the U.S. Air Force to use RAF Fairford for limited defensive strikes against Iranian missile capabilities. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps named RAF Fairford in July when it said that any British base used for attacks on Iranian territory would be considered a "legitimate target."

33e1d7779a:c97bcb60bb54f8af.title: Exclusive: Cornell rape allegations fuel House Democratic women's Title IX push
33e1d7779a:c97bcb60bb54f8af.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:c97bcb60bb54f8af.summary: A criminal investigation into allegations that a Cornell University student was gang raped by seven fraternity members in 2024 is fueling a new push by House Democratic women to strengthen federal protections against sexual violence on college campuses. Why it matters: The Democratic Women's Caucus is calling on congressional Republicans and the Trump administration to strengthen Title IX protections, arguing that the administration's changes to the civil rights law could leave students more vulnerable. The push comes just two days after the Trump administration rescinded Biden-era sex discrimination Title IX regulations and reinstated rules adopted during President Trump's first term. The Democratic Women's Caucus argues those changes have "eroded the processes in place for sexual misconduct investigations." Driving the news: "Her story should be a wake-up call Republicans cannot ignore: we need stronger protections and systems for survivors, and we need to act now," Democratic Women's Caucus Chair Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) and Vice Chairs Emilia Sykes (D-Ohio) and Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.) said in a statement first shared with Axios. The lawmakers argue the Cornell case underscores the need for stronger federal protections and more aggressive enforcement of Title IX, the landmark law barring sex discrimination at federally funded schools that also governs how schools respond to sexual harassment and assault allegations. They called on the administration and Republicans to "condemn what took place at Cornell, stand in solidarity with Jane Doe, and work with us to better protect survivors and ensure they can seek justice." Catch up quick: A former Cornell University student, referred to as "Jane Doe" in legal documents, is suing the school, seven Chi Phi fraternity members and others over allegations that she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in October of 2024. Cornell conducted a Title IX investigation after "Jane Doe" reported the incident in…

33e1d7779a:b6e3d08624e58848.title: Tennessee inmate Christa Pike's execution halted an hour beforehand
33e1d7779a:b6e3d08624e58848.author: Adam Tamburin
33e1d7779a:b6e3d08624e58848.summary: Death row inmate Christa Pike got a last-minute reprieve Wednesday when a federal appeals court stopped her execution about an hour before it was set to take place in Nashville. The latest: The court ordered "a short stay of execution" just before 9am CDT so it could consider an ongoing legal battle between Pike's attorneys and the state. Pike's attorneys argue her history of child sexual abuse wasn't presented to the jury before she was sentenced to death in 1996. Between the lines: The order stops Wednesday's execution and puts it on hold while the court considers this motion. The state supreme court could still set another execution date in the future depending on the outcome of this legal fight. What they're saying: "The interests of justice and the finality of Pike's impending execution compel the entry of a short stay of execution in order to properly analyze the parties' fully briefed arguments and resolve the issues on the merits," the court wrote. Two members of a three-judge panel backed the order. The third judge disagreed, describing the legal fight as a "last-ditch meritless effort to delay a lawful execution." Zoom in: Pike, the only woman on Tennessee's death row, was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 at the time. Two other people were convicted in the case, but only Pike got the death penalty. Pike's advocates do not contest her guilt, but they argue that her history of childhood abuse should have been presented to the jury during the sentencing phase as "important context and mitigation for the offense."

33e1d7779a:199d51294ee7e1ac.title: Trump's AI "constitution" crowns day of accelerating ambition
33e1d7779a:199d51294ee7e1ac.author: Zachary Basu
33e1d7779a:199d51294ee7e1ac.summary: With America's tech titans crowded around a single White House table Tuesday, President Trump extracted what he called a "morally binding" compact on AI safety. The terms were simple: Press ahead, project optimism and police yourselves. Why it matters: The White House Accord on Super Intelligence , signed by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia, formalizes industry self-regulation as Washington's response to the most alarming run of AI safety failures yet . Zoom in: Trump, who increasingly treats American AI dominance as central to his legacy, cast the accord as proof that an industry fractured over safety can still govern itself. He compared the document to "a constitution," claimed there was "a lot of commonality" among the tech leaders, and praised what he described as "tremendous self-policing." The one-page pact, which is deliberately light-touch, calls for "four layers of controls and auditing," including outside evaluators and independent board oversight. Between the lines: The accord makes a vague reference to future "laws or regulations," preserving the possibility of a tougher federal regime if ultimately needed. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, a MAGA bogeyman and the industry's most prominent advocate for slowing frontier development, signed the pact but stressed to reporters that it was only "a start." Trump AI adviser David Sacks, by contrast, treated the accord as mission accomplished — declaring on X that the companies were "accepting responsibility" for AI safety thanks to Trump's leadership. Zoom out: The White House pact capped an extraordinary day for the AI race across three capitals of American power. 1. In Washington, Trump spent Tuesday pulling AI deeper into both the machinery and mythology of his presidency. In the morning, he unveiled America.gov , an AI-powered front door to federal services, and vowed not to "stifle" a technology he says will eclipse the Industrial Revolution. Hours later, Trump signed an executive order…

33e1d7779a:7517f17b4d784505.title: AI agents have a normal-people problem
33e1d7779a:7517f17b4d784505.author: Shane Savitsky
33e1d7779a:7517f17b4d784505.summary: AI companies are staking their future on the mass adoption of agents , hoping that they can solve the annoyances of modern life — email, travel bookings, online purchases. Why it matters: The frenzy around Meta's Muse shows there's serious consumer curiosity about the technology. But most Americans live life beyond a computer screen and find much of their meaning outside of the 9-5. There's little evidence that they're willing to invest the time needed to re-engineer their lives in a way that puts AI at the center. And the more worrying issue for AI companies: What happens if people just don't want an assistant that leads them to do more work or allows them to be more productive? Driving the news: Muse vaulted to the top of Apple's App Store on the back of its integrations with Facebook and Instagram and a cute, fuzzy mascot . Meta expanded it to business customers, too. Muse's early success has given the industry hope that there's potential for the tech to break through. Meta isn't alone. Microsoft released a souped-up Copilot with an agentic Autopilot feature, folding more advanced AI into the workplace. And OpenAI announced its own agentic assistant, dots, this week. The big roadblock is that most Americans don't use AI chatbots, let alone agents. Back in February, Pew found that 51% avoided using AI chatbots entirely. Of those people, 79% who didn't use chatbots cited privacy concerns and 67% were unlikely to use a chatbot in the next year. The even bigger problem: Agents only become truly useful when people hand them access to their digital lives — and people really don't want to. A huge international Thales poll this year found broad pushback against the core uses of agents — only 13% of respondents would let an "AI helper" read their emails, 11% would let one rebook travel and just 7% would let it move money between bank accounts. Even shopping is a no-go: 56% told YouGov they wouldn't let an agent shop for them at all. Only 10% trust one with more than $25…

33e1d7779a:0cf48660ca5d3eae.title: Renewables boom faces a Trump-era cliff
33e1d7779a:0cf48660ca5d3eae.author: Amy Harder
33e1d7779a:0cf48660ca5d3eae.summary: America is adding record amounts of clean power despite President Trump's opposition to wind and solar — but the industry's top trade group warns the growth could fall off a "cliff" as soon as 2028. Why it matters: The disconnect illustrates the long lag between energy policy and what actually gets built, raising the stakes for a bipartisan permitting deal under negotiation now in the Senate. State of play: Wind and solar development is still benefiting from favorable economics and projects launched before Trump returned to the White House, Jason Grumet, CEO of the American Clean Power Association, told Axios. "If the administration continues to block the permitting of clean power, you'll start to see a cliff," said Grumet, who said the drop could become apparent in 2028 or 2029. Driving the news: Senate negotiators are expected to unveil a bipartisan deal to speed energy permitting as soon as Wednesday, though any final vote isn't expected until after the midterm elections. Between the lines: Democrats have sought assurances that the administration would allow stalled wind and solar projects to advance in exchange for supporting broader permitting changes. Grumet called the apparent agreement "encouraging," citing its technology-neutral approach and provisions for administration approval of wind projects. "Passage before the end of the year is essential," he said. By the numbers: Wind and solar account for nearly two-thirds of the new power capacity developers plan to add to the U.S. grid this year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The first half of 2026 was a record for new wind, solar and battery capacity, Grumet's group reported earlier this month. The White House says those numbers reflect policies Trump has already changed. When presented with the EIA figures at an Axios event last week , Jarrod Agen, executive director of the White House National Energy Dominance Council, said: "That's a carryover from the policies of the past." The…

33e1d7779a:de8ee90deb5e9c4c.title: OpenAI debuts "dots" as industry safety focus shifts to "What did my AI assistant do now?"
33e1d7779a:de8ee90deb5e9c4c.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:de8ee90deb5e9c4c.summary: OpenAI is equipping high-end subscribers with always-on agents, known as Dots . It's a bold move from a company that continues to deal with reports of its agents breaking past intended safeguards. Why it matters: AI's safety challenge has moved from "Will the chatbot say something harmful?" to "How can we stop autonomous agents from attempting hacks online?" to "Uh-oh, what did my AI assistant do now?" Driving the news: The unveiling of Dots was the signature debut among a flurry of announcements at OpenAI's developer conference on Tuesday. Think of a Dot as an AI assistant running on its own virtual computer in the cloud. It can browse the web, use connected apps, create files and run tools while keeping track of a project over time. Dots can be summoned on mobile devices or computers and work across connected apps, browsers and their own virtual computer. The big picture: Dots (like Meta's Muse ) are being launched publicly despite a spate of revelations about agents from OpenAI and other AI companies taking unintended actions. In just the last few days, OpenAI has been making fresh disclosures of unintended behavior and apologizing to Australia for hacking into its Medicare system's websites. OpenAI also said this week it was scrapping an update to its most powerful Astra model after it failed to meet safety thresholds. Between the lines: It's not the first time OpenAI has been at the center of safety concerns. In the early days of ChatGPT, much of the focus was on the potential for dangerous discussions, such as encouraging suicide or eating disorders, issues for which OpenAI faces multiple lawsuits. Now, the conversation is shifting to potentially harmful agentic actions. In the most serious security incident to date, OpenAI's agents were behind a July attack on Hugging Face. What they're saying: OpenAI leaders expressed confidence that the Dots it is sending into the world won't run amok. The company said Dots include safeguards from ChatGPT and Codex, plus…

33e1d7779a:5772805a514e9fb6.title: U.S.-Iran talks yield little, raising odds of renewed combat
33e1d7779a:5772805a514e9fb6.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:5772805a514e9fb6.summary: Efforts this week by Qatari mediators to broker a diplomatic breakthrough between the U.S. and Iran have made little progress, with neither side willing to budge, according to three sources familiar with the talks. Why it matters: The stalemate bolsters the belief on both sides that a renewed military conflict is becoming more likely. U.S. officials think President Trump could order a return to major combat operations after the midterms. Qatari officials will keep trying but are growing increasingly frustrated with both sides, two of the sources said. Driving the news: Qatari mediator Ali al-Thawadi met Monday with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his team in New York for several hours. A source with knowledge said they discussed a two-page Qatari compromise proposal. According to two other sources, the Qatari plan was aimed at addressing both Iran's demand for lifting the U.S. naval blockade and the U.S. demand for Iranian nuclear concessions. On Monday evening, al-Thawadi held talks in Washington with Trump envoy Jared Kushner and other U.S. officials. Vice President Vance also attended a small part of the meeting. The White House declined to comment. The intrigue: On Monday morning, the White House was hopeful of progress. U.S. officials briefed several media outlets, including Axios, that the talks were "positive and constructive" and that Iran "indicated they are flexible on the nuclear issues." The officials even said Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds in return for concrete steps to pare back its nuclear program. But several hours later, while the Qatari officials were still at the White House, Trump posted on Truth Social that he offered nothing to Iran. State of play: One of the sources said there was no significant movement in the talks on Monday. "It is stuck. The Iranians are asking for things the U.S. can't accept and the U.S. thinks it is winning so there is no need for compromise," the source said.…

33e1d7779a:9e8939ac5e617973.title: Boeing nabs $20B contract for Navy's futuristic fighter
33e1d7779a:9e8939ac5e617973.author: Colin Demarest
33e1d7779a:9e8939ac5e617973.summary: Boeing will build the U.S. Navy's next fighter aircraft, following years of clandestine competition and multiple contracting false alarms. Why it matters: Boeing's win in the F/A-XX competition means the company's sixth-generation aircraft will succeed the Super Hornet fleet, long relied upon and recently employed across the Middle East. The company is also constructing the Air Force's F-47, previously unveiled in an Oval Office address featuring President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The latest: The Pentagon announced the deal Tuesday. It's worth more than $20 billion. It comes after months of squabbling between the White House, Pentagon, lawmakers and industry. Its ups and downs and rumored award timelines were closely watched by defense analysts and reporters. Context: Boeing bested Northrop Grumman. Lockheed Martin was previously knocked out of the running. Executives from both companies had told Axios they were confident in their offerings. State of play: Little has been revealed about the warplane's final design. But it will complement the F-35, of which there are short-takeoff and carrier variants. What they're saying: Former Navy Secretary John Phelan in December told Axios that F/A-XX was, in fact, not dead. He previously told lawmakers the warplane would ensure naval air dominance. Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle advocated for the project during his nomination hearing, telling lawmakers the service "must have an air wing that is comprised of the most advanced strike fighters." And Caudle's predecessor, Lisa Franchetti , suggested it would sport "advanced sensors, advanced lethality, advanced range" and be able to "integrate with manned and unmanned capabilities." More from Axios: American airpower F/A-XX decision must be "made quickly," Navy chief says Trump administration shelves Navy's F/A-XX, citing industry strain

33e1d7779a:c5a3e8a5a21ac027.title: Trump floats Jay Clayton as AI czar as he looks to fill the position in days
33e1d7779a:c5a3e8a5a21ac027.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:c5a3e8a5a21ac027.summary: President Trump on Tuesday told Axios Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton would be a good AI czar. Why it matters : Trump is actively looking to fill the position as calls for government intervention on AI intensify. Driving the news : As the director of national intelligence, Clayton is the president's principle intelligence adviser that sits atop the 18-agency intelligence community. During his July confirmation hearing , Clayton said that, similarly to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's approach, for the intelligence community "it resonates that AI is not only an opportunity but a threat." "When something's both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it," Clayton said. Asked who he wants to be AI czar, Trump said: "I have somebody in mind." Clayton is "a good man. He's right here. That's a good idea," Trump added when prompted. The precise duties of the czar have yet to be spelled out , although Trump earlier said he wants to create the AI Force, a new government agency. Trump told reporters outside the White House he wants to pick someone in the next three or four days. Trump, House Speaker Mike Johnson and AI executives met today to discuss balancing AI innovation and safety and encourage compoanies to regulate themselves and each other. Catch up quick : Silicon Valley players and venture capitalist David Sacks, who also attended Tuesday's meeting, previously held the AI czar role. Sacks left that post in March after his special government employee status ran out but continued to exert influence from an outside advisory role.

33e1d7779a:79bac6a5abba1621.title: Trump, top AI leaders agree to voluntary ​AI ​standards
33e1d7779a:79bac6a5abba1621.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:79bac6a5abba1621.summary: President Trump said Tuesday that top AI executives agreed to voluntary standards aimed at increasing industry oversight. Why it matters: The agreement puts AI companies at the center of policing their own technology as pressure grows for stronger safeguards. Driving the news: Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson announced Tuesday afternoon that several AI titans signed a voluntary agreement, which they called an "accord," outlining standards for reviewing AI systems. "This starts with every company that is training and deploying frontier models having robust internal processes and controls," the accord reads. "This is a statement of principles ... a statement of standards, commitments that are voluntary on behalf of the industry. It sets forth expectations," Johnson told reporters. "That's important because you need people to be providing oversight and transparency, and that's what these leaders are going to do." Trump also announced a name change for the technology, rebranding AI as "SI," or super intelligence. Zoom in: Mark Zuckerberg outlined some of the steps participating companies expect to take, including internal risk reviews and outside audits. He said the leaders drafted a list of principles that include reviewing internal controls and detecting issues with the technology, which could include multiple layers of auditing controls. He said there will be internal risk review and external auditors to examine the technology. The Information reported that top AI labs Anthropic, OpenAI and Google were working together before the White House meeting on a self-regulation framework to coordinate on "testing and auditing the technology." Friction point: Sources who work in AI told Axios they were concerned self-policing would not solve the safety problem currently embroiling the industry. The agreement's scope and enforcement remain unclear because full details have not yet been released. When asked for comment Tuesday, the White House told Axios: "Turn on TRUTH…

33e1d7779a:1eef151c513c9db4.summary: The Supreme Court will allow the Trump administration's policy to deport immigrants to "third " to continue and will consider the legal question at a later date. The big picture: The policy of expelling migrants to countries that are not their home country has faced legal challenges from early in the president's second term — and the Supreme Court has once again cleared the administration's way. 33e1d7779a:ba20d63ef6d545b9.title: Trump leans on SCOTUS shadow docket more than Biden, Obama and Bush combined
33e1d7779a:ba20d63ef6d545b9.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:ba20d63ef6d545b9.summary: President Trump's administration on Monday filed its 41st application to the Supreme Court's shadow docket , a milestone that matches the total number of petitions it filed during his entire first term — in less than two years. Why it matters: The record highlights how often the president has turned to SCOTUS to secure authority to temporarily revive policies blocked by lower courts. What they're saying: "We have never seen an administration run to the Supreme Court with the speed and numbers that we're seeing out of the Trump administration this term," Stephen Spaulding, managing director of the Kohlberg Center at the Brennan Center for Justice, tells Axios. "Keep in mind that the shadow docket, the emergency docket, is used and should be used for actual emergencies," he says. "The administration continues to claim that they're going to face irreparable harm, and that this is an appropriate emergency for the Supreme Court to review, which we think, calls into question how the court's using the shadow docket in the first place." The White House and the Justice Department did not immediately respond to Axios' requests for comment. How it works: The emergency, or shadow, docket lets parties seek expedited Supreme Court intervention before a case completes the ordinary appeals process. The court can, for example, pause a lower court's injunction and allow a policy to take effect while litigation continues. The orders are often issued unsigned and without explanation, complicating how lower court judges apply the orders to future cases. By the numbers: The second Trump administration filed its 41st emergency application Monday. The Biden administration made 19 requests over four years. The Obama and George W. Bush administrations made eight requests over their combined 16 years in office. Obama made three, and Bush made five. Driving the news: The 41st application asked the court to allow the Bureau of Prisons to reimplement a policy cutting off some gender-affirming…

33e1d7779a:ca5628092aecde42.title: OpenAI hit with landmark lawsuit following Hugging Face hack
33e1d7779a:ca5628092aecde42.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:ca5628092aecde42.summary: A public interest law group hit OpenAI with a lawsuit Tuesday over its breach of tech company Hugging Face , seeking court-ordered restrictions to prevent future hacks. The big picture: The rogue hacking incident — and reports of tens of thousands of other possible examples of problematic agentic behavior — demonstrated the urgent risk of AI agents escaping their testing environments, bypassing guardrails and outpacing their creators . The case tests an increasingly urgent question as AI agents gain power: Who bears legal responsibility when an agent blows past its guardrails and causes real-world harm? Driving the news: " OpenAI is responsible for the conduct of its agents," Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology (LASST), representing itself alongside Gerstein Harrow LLP, argued in its suit filed in California Superior Court Tuesday. They allege OpenAI agents "knowingly" accessed Hugging Face without permission and that employees or officers caused that access "either with actual knowledge or in willful blindness." The suit aims to block development practices that allow AI agents to autonomously cause outside harm, LASST founder Tyler Whitmer tells Axios and ensures there are "legal mechanisms that tie these harms back to a responsible human" or corporate actor when an AI agent causes harm. Whitmer hopes an injunction would "incentivize OpenAI and … the industry to alter their development processes in a way that would prevent this from happening" again. Zoom in: The organization sued under California's Unfair Competition Law , arguing OpenAI's "unlawful and unfair business practices" diverted work and resources to responding to the Hugging Face incident. It also argued "OpenAI's insistence on externalizing the harms of its unsafe decision-making is a fundamentally unfair business practice," nodding to a letter from OpenAI and other tech leaders calling on organizations to "[m]ake cyber defense an immediate leadership priority." The suit also argued…

ecbefe1924:a58a8203f9eb453d.title: Beyond the Paycheck: Using Fringe Benefits to Attract a Broader Pool of Applicants
ecbefe1924:a58a8203f9eb453d.author: Thea S. Zoellner
ecbefe1924:a58a8203f9eb453d.summary: Many firms in tight labor markets recruit for highly gender-segregated occupations, leaving them, in effect, drawing from only half the potential labor pool. We study how firms can use fringe benefits to attract workers and influence occupational choice. Unlike occupation-specific recruiting strategies, fringe benefits can be added to any occupation; they are also easily tailored, implemented, and scaled. Using a personalized and incentivized discrete choice experiment, we present participants with job options that match their skills and work task preferences. Within each option, we vary salary, occupation, and fringe benefits that adolescents had classified as gender-neutral, male-typed, or female-typed. We find that fringe benefits are highly valued: their effect is around a third as large as having prior interest in the occupation. Neutral and stereotypical benefits in particular improve perceptions of the firm across multiple dimensions. Furthermore, we find substantial gender differences. Female-typed benefits deter male participants, whereas all other benefit-participant combinations have a positive effect. Female participants value benefits more when those benefits are paired with an atypical occupation, and we find suggestive evidence that this reflects benefits alleviating concerns about limited support in such roles. In addition, male-typed benefits can increase the attractiveness of gender-atypical occupations for female participants. Female participants who consider atypical occupations place relatively higher value on these benefits and tend to exhibit less traditionally feminine preferences. We also find suggestive evidence that anticipated social reactions, particularly from parents, accompany these choices.

ecbefe1924:b320ea52cb495871.title: How to Increase the Mental Well-Being of Your Employees? An Overview of Research Testing Interventions in the Workplace
ecbefe1924:b320ea52cb495871.author: Baert, Stijn
ecbefe1924:b320ea52cb495871.summary: This systematic literature review provides a state-of-the-art overview of the effectiveness of workplace interventions aimed at improving workersâ€™ mental well-being. Specifically, it examines which types of interventions are effective for which aspects of mental well-being, both in the short and long term. To this end, we identify 125 randomised controlled trials comprising 147 interventions that vary in their objectives (prevention, treatment, or reintegration), targets (workers or work), methods (cognitive, meditation-based, physical, ergonomic, organisational, or multimethod) and delivery channels (offline, online or hybrid). Mental well-being outcomes are classified as biological and self-reported indicators of the three components of subjective mental well-being (evaluative, affective, and eudaimonic well-being). Overall, we find that, for preventing and treating early mental health symptoms, cognitive or meditation-based interventions targeting personal coping resources appear most promising. In contrast, successful reintegration seems to require a combination of cognitive and organisational interventions, with the latter addressing job demands and resources.

ecbefe1924:131e88a7c1c49d4f.title: Meetings
ecbefe1924:131e88a7c1c49d4f.author: Yaling Xu
ecbefe1924:131e88a7c1c49d4f.summary: Why do we have so many meetings? Few workplace features are so scorned, yet seemingly so necessary. This paper provides the first large-scale economic evidence on workplace meetings using an original survey of more than 9, 000 workers linked to matched employer–employee administrative data from Norway. We show that meetings are both common and costly, consuming an average of 12 percent of work hours and 14 percent of firm wage bills. Planning, problem solving, information sharing, and project coordination account for the majority of meeting activity. High-paying and high-revenue firms devote more resources to meetings despite facing a substantially higher opportunity cost of employee time. Meeting frequency and intensity are positively related to worker wage growth. Workers in meeting-intensive firms report greater on-the-job learning, and interactions with more senior colleagues are associated with stronger wage growth, suggesting that knowledge transmission within firms is an important mechanism. Meetings are the broccoli of work – widely disliked, but probably good for us anyway.

ecbefe1924:3445fc66ea310c41.title: Signals, Steps, and Setbacks: Age Discrimination in a Laddered Labor Market
ecbefe1924:3445fc66ea310c41.author: Xiaoyu Xia
ecbefe1924:3445fc66ea310c41.summary: We study age discrimination in a labor market with a job ladder, where worker productivity is revealed over time. Using data from a large Chinese recruitment platform that links job postings, applications, and employer responses, we document sharp declines in applications and callbacks at posted age cutoffs. Discrimination operates in both directions: older applicants are disadvantaged in entry-level jobs, while younger applicants are less likely to be hired into managerial roles. A model of statistical discrimination with imperfect signal screening explains these patterns. Consistent with the model, older applicants to entry-level jobs are negatively selected relative to their peers.

ecbefe1924:92bf3f127abbc04d.title: Female-Targeted Hiring Subsidies, Firm Learning, and Women’s Employment
ecbefe1924:92bf3f127abbc04d.author: Anna Raute
ecbefe1924:92bf3f127abbc04d.summary: Women often struggle to re-enter employment after career breaks, possibly because employers are uncertain about their productivity. We study whether hiring subsidies help firms overcome this uncertainty and hire from this group. Exploiting an Italian policy that temporarily cut payroll taxes for women hired from non-employment, we find that firms persistently hire more women with career breaks, including mothers, following subsidy adoption. Consistent with employer learning about target-group productivity, firms with better initial matches later hire more from this group. Subsidized workers also show stronger labor-market attachment. These findings suggest demand-side interventions can complement supply-side policies in addressing gender gaps.

b3ea4f41ab:6d32517dc3ca1324.title: Daily Team Behaviors as Predictors of Team Effectiveness Outcomes: Evidence from a Technology Entrepreneurship Incubator Program
b3ea4f41ab:6d32517dc3ca1324.author: Sommerville, Gillian
b3ea4f41ab:6d32517dc3ca1324.summary: Team effectiveness in high-stakes, time-limited work contexts remains an underexplored area of organizational and applied psychology research. This study examined whether daily process behaviors—specifically team communication and collaboration—predict end-of-program team effectiveness outcomes in the context of an intensive, eight-week technology entrepreneurship incubator program. Participants were members of five start-up teams enrolled in the start-up program at a large research university. As part of a larger mixed-methods study, participants completed daily diary measures of team communication and collaboration using a digital platform (Metricwire) for 15 days. At program end, participants completed a post-program survey assessing team effectiveness outcomes including creativity, psychological safety, team viability, collective efficacy, authentic relationships, opportunities for growth, and program satisfaction. Simple linear regressions revealed that daily collaboration significantly predicted creativity, psychological safety, team viability, and collective efficacy. Daily communication similarly predicted creativity and psychological safety. Authentic relationships were not significantly predicted by either behavioral measure. These findings contribute to the growing literature on team process and performance by demonstrating that observable daily team behaviors capture meaningful variance in team effectiveness outcomes, Implications for team-based intervention design and digital measurement methodology are discussed.

b3ea4f41ab:9dc5a2ab510ffd27.title: Staged financing beyond the venture record: Equity rounds in the accounts of Italian SMEs
b3ea4f41ab:9dc5a2ab510ffd27.author: Plantamura, Antonio Volpe
b3ea4f41ab:9dc5a2ab510ffd27.summary: Almost everything known about equity rounds in young firms comes from the records of professional investors, so the evidence is selected on the presence of an intermediary. We read rounds instead from the share-premium reserve, a compulsory, disclosed and restricted line of the Italian statutory balance sheet, for 3, 225 certified innovative SMEs over 2016–2025: 2, 991 priced capital increases on 1, 330 firms. Firms about to raise grew twice as fast in the preceding year and held identical cash, yet six in ten closed it at a loss; profitability falls and intangible assets rise only after the round. Seven panel estimators place the association across firms and not within them; a taxonomy estimated blind to the event finds the mechanism in all five financial configurations, with incidence differing eightfold; six flexible learners fail to improve on the linear specification. Selection operates on growth, not on profitability, a distinction intermediated samples cannot see.
